mcqs.question: Why does a live leaderboard's rank-read QPS typically far exceed its score-update QPS?
options: Rank reads are computationally cheaper, so the system generates more of them automatically
Score updates are batched and only counted once per day
Players check standings (their rank, the top N) far more often than they actually finish a scoring event
This ratio is specific to leaderboards and never happens in other read-heavy systems
mcqs.explanation: Users check rankings much more frequently than they generate new scores, producing a read-heavy skew similar to other systems in this group (like a URL shortener's clicks vs creates). Read cost doesn't cause more reads to happen; updates aren't artificially batched daily; and this read-heavy pattern is common across many systems, not unique to leaderboards.

mcqs.question: Why is a sorted set (skip list) generally preferred over a B-tree-indexed score column for a live leaderboard?
options: B-trees cannot store numeric scores
Sorted sets require no memory at all
B-tree indexes are deprecated in modern databases
A sorted set offers both cheap score updates and a native, cheap "rank of X" query, which most SQL B-tree indexes don't provide directly
mcqs.explanation: A sorted set gives O(log n) updates and a native rank operation; a typical B-tree index speeds up range scans and ordering but has no built-in "what's the rank of this value" query, often forcing a costly scan. B-trees handle numbers fine and aren't deprecated; sorted sets still consume memory proportional to their size.

mcqs.question: In a sharded leaderboard, why can't a user's global rank be computed from their local shard alone?
options: Local shard rank is always identical to global rank
Global rank also depends on how many higher scores exist across every other shard, which the local shard doesn't know
Shards do not support rank queries at all
Global rank requires re-sharding the entire user base on every query
mcqs.explanation: A user's true global rank depends on scores in every shard, not just their own — the fix is maintaining small periodically-refreshed aggregates per shard rather than querying every shard live on each request. Shards do support local rank queries fine, and this doesn't require re-sharding anything.

mcqs.question: A fitness app's leaderboard rank is refreshed every few seconds instead of being computed live on every request. What's the trade-off being made?
options: Trading a small amount of rank freshness for lower per-query cost, which is imperceptible for most consumer use cases
Trading correctness for faster score updates
Trading storage cost for compute cost
There is no trade-off — periodic refresh is strictly worse in every dimension
mcqs.explanation: Periodic refresh accepts rank being a few seconds stale in exchange for cheaper rank queries — a trade most users never notice. It doesn't affect score-update correctness, and it isn't purely a storage-vs-compute trade; nor is it strictly worse, since it materially reduces query cost.

mcqs.question: Why does re-sorting the entire user list on every score update fail to scale?
options: It's forbidden by most database engines
The cost per update scales with total user count (O(n log n)), rather than with the size of the single change that occurred
It only works for scores under 1,000 points
It requires a distributed transaction across all shards
mcqs.explanation: A full re-sort's cost depends on how many users exist in total, not on how small the actual change was — at millions of users and frequent updates, that cost per write becomes untenable. This isn't forbidden by databases, isn't limited by score magnitude, and doesn't inherently require distributed transactions.
